ARREARS::transferee-liability.code: Electricity Act / Supply Codes (general principle; cf. Clause 4.3(g)&(h))
ARREARS::transferee-liability.topic: Arrears are not a charge; transferee liable only where statutory rules/terms so provide

cases.title: Haryana State Electricity Board v. M/s Hanuman Rice Mills, Dhanauri & Ors.
cases.topic: Arrears are not a charge; transferee liable only where statutory rules/terms so provide
cases.holding: (i) Electricity arrears do not constitute a charge over the property, so in general law a transferee cannot be made liable for the previous owner/occupier's dues. (ii) But where statutory rules, or statutory terms and conditions of supply, authorise the supplier to demand the previous owner's arrears from a purchaser seeking re-/fresh connection, the supplier may recover them. Here the Board pleaded no such enabling provision (introduced in Haryana only in 2001), so the demand against the auction-purchaser failed.
cases.flag: Multi-state (Haryana) and general-law principle; the doctrinal foundation of the arrears/transferee cluster (cf. SCJ-005 K.C. Ninan, SCJ-012). The Court expressly notes that provisions like Clause 4.3(g) & (h) of an Electricity Supply Code are necessary to enable such recovery.

cases.title: K.C. Ninan v. Kerala State Electricity Board & Ors.
cases.neutral_citation: (2023) SCC OnLine SC 603; Civil Appeal Nos. 2109-2110 of 2004 (batch)
cases.topic: Supply Code can create a statutory charge for a previous owner's arrears recoverable from a new owner (apex authority)
cases.holding: Yes. A condition of supply requiring the new owner to clear the previous owner's arrears has a statutory character (s.49, 1948 Act); the State Commission's regulatory power under s.50, and the rule-making power under s.181 read with s.50, are wide enough to stipulate recovery of a previous owner's arrears from a new/subsequent owner and to create a statutory charge on the premises even where the plenary statute does not provide for one. Such Supply Code recoupment has a reasonable nexus with the objects of the 2003 Act. The power to recover by suit is independent of the disconnection power under s.56; and 'as is where is' puts an auction-purchaser on notice of electricity dues. Outstanding interest from the date of the supply application was waived under Article 142.
cases.flag: Apex authority confirming the arrears/transferee line (cf. SCJ-031 Haryana SEB; applied in SCJ-005 Amir Ahmad). Substantially qualifies Isha Marbles (1995).

CPC::res-judicata.topic: Second suit on a different subject-matter/relief not barred

cases.title: Haryana State Electricity Board v. M/s Hanuman Rice Mills, Dhanauri & Ors.
cases.topic: Second suit on a different subject-matter/relief not barred
cases.holding: The second suit (challenging the 1998 disconnection threat and disconnection for the previous owner's arrears) was not barred by res judicata by the dismissal of the earlier suit (for a permanent injunction against the 1995 demand), the matters directly in issue and the reliefs being different.

EA2003::126.code: Electricity Act, 2003 (read with the DERC Supply Code Regulations)
EA2003::126.topic: Legal fiction of 'deemed' consumption under the Supply Code / s.126 must be given full effect

cases.title: BSES Rajdhani Power Ltd. v. Delhi Electricity Regulatory Commission
cases.topic: Legal fiction of 'deemed' consumption under the Supply Code / s.126 must be given full effect
cases.holding: Yes. Where the statute and the DERC Supply Code Regulations create a legal fiction that assessed energy is 'deemed' consumed (e.g. under the LDHF formula), the fiction must be taken to its logical end: the assessed units must be treated as 'sales'. The DERC's method of back-calculating units from the reduced settlement amount is contrary to law; assessed energy is to be considered as supply, with the impact and carrying costs allowed.

cases.title: Islam v. State of U.P. & 4 Others
cases.topic: Agricultural ancillary use (kolhu) within sanctioned load is not unauthorised use
cases.holding: No. Ancillary use of a sanctioned agricultural connection for a kolhu/kutti machine to crush one's own produce, within the sanctioned load, is authorised agricultural use (per the licensee's own policy order of 11.11.2005), not unauthorised use — unless the load exceeds the sanctioned load or a second meter is installed. The burden to prove commercial use/theft is on the department; absent any allegation of crushing for others/hire, excess load, or a second meter, the assessment is illegal and quashed.

cases.title: Kapil Gupta v. U.P. Power Corpn. Ltd. & Anr.
cases.topic: A Section 126 assessment can be made even in a theft case
cases.holding: Section 126 (Chapter XII, investigation/enforcement) empowers a provisional assessment of charges for unauthorised use, while Section 135 (Chapter XIV, offences) makes unauthorised use a criminal offence; the two operate in different chapters, and a person committing theft/unauthorised use still bears the civil liability to pay for the consumption. A provisional assessment can therefore be made in a theft case.

cases.title: Executive Engineer, Southern Electricity Supply Co. of Orissa Ltd. (SOUTHCO) v. Sri Seetaram Rice Mill
cases.topic: Sections 126 and 135 are distinct provisions in different fields; s.126 is civil and intention-neutral
cases.holding: No commonality. Sections 126 and 135 operate in different and distinct fields. Section 135 falls within criminal jurisprudence and mens rea is a relevant factor for theft; Section 126 does not speak of any criminal intendment and is primarily a civil remedy, applying even in the absence of intention.

cases.title: Executive Engineer, Southern Electricity Supply Co. of Orissa Ltd. (SOUTHCO) v. Sri Seetaram Rice Mill
cases.topic: 'Unauthorised use' is a wider, purposively-construed expression covering excess load
cases.holding: 'Unauthorised use of electricity' is an expression of wider connotation, to be construed purposively rather than restrictively by the clauses of the Explanation, keeping in mind the object and purpose of the Act. Consumption in excess of the maximum contracted/sanctioned load falls under Explanation (b)(iv) to Section 126 (besides violating the Regulations and the agreement of supply).

cases.title: West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd. (WBSEDCL) v. M/s Orion Metal Pvt. Ltd.
cases.topic: Theft (s.135) is a subset of unauthorised use (s.126); a s.126 assessment is available even in theft cases
cases.holding: Yes. All instances of unauthorised use may not amount to theft, but theft under Section 135 falls within the definition of 'unauthorised use of electricity'; use through a tampered meter is therefore unauthorised use assessable under Section 126(6)(b)(iii). The authorities are empowered to make a provisional and final assessment under Section 126(1) even in cases where electricity is unauthorisedly used by way of theft.

cases.title: Lalit Kumar Kapoor v. Kanpur Electricity Supply Company & Anr.
cases.topic: Law applicable to the deposit condition and assessment rate is the law in force on the date of the FINAL assessment, not the date of provisional assessment or the underlying cause of action
cases.holding: The amended Act governs. A provisional assessment is not a final assessment and carries no independent right of appeal; the cause of action for the statutory appeal arises only from the final assessment. The law prevailing on the date of the final assessment (here, 2011) applies both to the deposit condition for the appeal and to the assessment rate under Section 126(6) (amended to 'twice' the tariff, from 'one-and-half times'), regardless of when the theft/cause of action arose (2004) or the provisional assessment was made.

cases.title: M.D., Pakshimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Electricity Ombudsman & Anr.
cases.topic: CGRF and Ombudsman have no jurisdiction over Section 126 unauthorised-use assessments or Section 127 appellate orders — a parallel forum by subordinate legislation is impermissible
cases.holding: No. The Assessing Officer under Section 126 is a statutory authority and his order is appealable only under Section 127; where the statute itself creates its own adjudicatory and appellate forum, a parallel forum created by subordinate legislation (CGRF/Ombudsman under the 2007 Regulations) is not permissible and has no jurisdiction at all over such assessments. An earlier writ order that had allowed the consumer to approach CGRF, without the jurisdictional point being raised or contested, does not confer jurisdiction — a judgment lays down a ratio decidendi only on an issue raised, argued and decided, and jurisdiction cannot be conferred by consent, acquiescence, or a court's assumption. The entire CGRF and Ombudsman proceedings (including the order refunding Rs. 14.44 lakh with 16% compound interest) were quashed as a nullity, with liberty to the consumer to pursue objections before the Assessing Officer under Section 126 or an appeal under Section 127, condoning any resulting delay if availed within one month.

EA2003::126(3).topic: Personal hearing is part of 'reasonable opportunity' before a final theft assessment

cases.title: Hazi Mohd. Yaseen v. P.V.V.N.L. & Another
cases.topic: Personal hearing is part of 'reasonable opportunity' before a final theft assessment
cases.holding: It requires a personal hearing. Merely taking note of written objections is not compliance; because supply (an essential service) has been disconnected and the theft charge carries penal consequences, a personal hearing is essential before a final assessment. The ex parte final assessment is quashed and remitted for a fresh reasoned order after personal hearing, conditioned on the consumer depositing 50% of the claim (25% cash + 25% security).

EA2003::126(5).topic: Assessment period — entire period of unauthorised use, or 12 months if unascertainable

cases.title: Hazi Mohd. Yaseen v. P.V.V.N.L. & Another
cases.topic: Assessment period — entire period of unauthorised use, or 12 months if unascertainable
cases.holding: Section 126(5) has two parts: assessment for the entire period during which unauthorised use took place, or, if that period cannot be ascertained, a period limited to twelve months preceding inspection. Whether the period (here 407 days) was properly ascertained is a factual question for the assessing/appellate authority.

EA2003::127.code: Electricity Act, 2003 (transition from U.P. Supply (Consumers) Regulations 1984 / U.P. Supply Code 2002)
EA2003::127.topic: Scope of the Section 127 appeal — confined to Section 126 orders; transitional assessments

cases.title: Aruna Bhargava v. PuVVNL & Another
cases.topic: Scope of the Section 127 appeal — confined to Section 126 orders; transitional assessments
cases.holding: No. Section 127(1) confines the appeal to a final order 'made under Section 126' of the 2003 Act; a pre-2003 assessment is not such an order, so neither Section 127 nor its pre-deposit condition applies. Section 185(2) & (5) (with Section 6 of the General Clauses Act) preserve the pre-2003 assessment and its appellate forum. The Commissioner's rejection under s.127(2) was without jurisdiction; the appeal is remitted to the forum under Regulations 1984 / Code 2002.
cases.flag: Multi-regime transitional case: it construes the pre-2005 U.P. regime (Regulations 1984 and U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2002), not the 2005 Code.

cases.title: Kapil Gupta v. U.P. Power Corpn. Ltd. & Anr.
cases.topic: Writ relegated to the statutory appeal where only factual disputes arise
cases.holding: Relegated to the appeal. Where the challenge to a Section 126 assessment raises only disputed questions of fact and no question of jurisdiction, vires, or breach of natural justice/fundamental rights, the writ court will not bypass the Section 127 appeal; the earlier decision on merits in this consumer's case turned on a four-year pendency, not any absolute rule, and Ashok Kumar (vires/jurisdiction) is distinguishable.

cases.title: Executive Engineer, Southern Electricity Supply Co. of Orissa Ltd. (SOUTHCO) v. Sri Seetaram Rice Mill
cases.topic: Sections 126-127 form a complete code; only a final Section 126(3) order is appealable; the High Court should not ordinarily interfere with a final assessment
cases.holding: Sections 126 and 127 together constitute a complete code. Only a final order of assessment under Section 126(3) is appealable under Section 127; a notice-cum-provisional assessment under Section 126(2) is not appealable. The High Court should normally decline to interfere under Article 226 with a final assessment — it may examine a jurisdictional challenge but must not travel into the assessing officer's exclusive domain of assessment and fact-finding.

cases.title: Lalit Kumar Kapoor v. Kanpur Electricity Supply Company & Anr.
cases.topic: Challenge to a final theft assessment relegated to the statutory appeal; pre-deposit not relaxed
cases.holding: Whether inspection or provisional assessment was properly made, and whether reasonable opportunity was given, are matters merged into the earlier writ proceeding that directed consideration of the representation (itself equivalent to the provisional stage) and cannot be reopened by a fresh writ against the final assessment; the final assessment must be challenged before the appellate authority under Section 127, and in a theft matter — given the public interest in the essential service of electricity — the Court will not relax the statutory deposit condition to enable the petitioner to avoid it.

EA2003::135.topic: Proof standard: civil for s.126 assessment, beyond reasonable doubt + mens rea for s.135 theft

cases.title: West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd. (WBSEDCL) v. M/s Orion Metal Pvt. Ltd.
cases.topic: Proof standard: civil for s.126 assessment, beyond reasonable doubt + mens rea for s.135 theft
cases.holding: To prove theft in a criminal proceeding the case must be proved beyond reasonable doubt with mens rea established; such strict proof is not necessary for assessing liability under Section 126(1), which requires only civil proof.

EA2003::145.code: Electricity Act, 2003 (with Supply Code 2005 & CGRF Regulations 2007)
EA2003::145.topic: Forum: consumer disputes (Code/civil-court bar) vs a non-consumer's tort claim (Lok Adalat)

cases.title: Divisional Engineer, Electricity Distribution Division-I v. Raman Singh & Another
cases.topic: Forum: consumer disputes (Code/civil-court bar) vs a non-consumer's tort claim (Lok Adalat)
cases.holding: For a consumer's dispute, the Act and the Supply Code are comprehensive and civil-court jurisdiction is barred by Section 145. A non-consumer's claim for tort damages against the licensee is not a Code/CGRF matter; 'supply of power' is a 'public utility service' under Section 22-A of the LSA Act, 1987, so the Permanent Lok Adalat has jurisdiction, and the CGRF/Ombudsman Regulations, 2007 (covering only consumer grievances) do not apply. The compensation award is upheld.

cases.title: Executive Engineer, Electricity Distribution Division-II v. State of U.P. & 2 Others
cases.topic: Forum: consumer disputes (Code/civil-court bar) vs a non-consumer's electrocution-damages claim (Lok Adalat)
cases.holding: Yes. 'Public utility service' (LSA Act s.22-A) means supply of power to the public and needs no consumer relationship; the Permanent Lok Adalat has adjudicatory power under s.22-C(8) where conciliation fails. A consumer's electricity dispute is cognizable only by the statutory authorities under the Act/Code, civil-court jurisdiction being barred by Section 145; but a non-consumer's tort claim for electrocution is a civil dispute the Lok Adalat may decide, and a weaker-section claimant cannot be relegated to a civil suit.

EA2003::152.topic: Compounding of electricity theft — whether a pending prosecution is required

cases.title: Abhinav Seva Sansthan Mahavidyalaya v. U.P. Power Corporation Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.topic: Compounding of electricity theft — whether a pending prosecution is required
cases.holding: Section 152(2) and (3) operate at different stages: under s.152(2), where no criminal proceeding has yet been instituted, payment of the compounding sum sets the person at liberty and bars institution of proceedings; s.152(3) (acceptance deemed an acquittal) applies only where a prosecution is already pending. Compounding therefore does not require a pending prosecution.
cases.flag: The judgment refers throughout to 'Section 152(2) of the Electricity Supply Code 2005'; Section 152 is in the Electricity Act, 2003. Recorded, not merged.

EA2003::154.topic: The Section 126 assessment and the Special Court's Section 154(5) civil-liability determination are not parallel/mutually exclusive — both may proceed

cases.title: West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd. (WBSEDCL) v. M/s Orion Metal Pvt. Ltd.
cases.topic: The Section 126 assessment and the Special Court's Section 154(5) civil-liability determination are not parallel/mutually exclusive — both may proceed
cases.holding: The Section 126(1) assessment power and the power to determine civil liability under Section 154(5) are not parallel to each other; the High Court erred in holding the two proceedings cannot operate parallelly. Where there is no theft (only unauthorised use), the loss is assessed under Section 126(1) alone; where the unauthorised use amounts to theft, a Section 126(1) assessment AND a Section 135 complaint may both proceed, with the Special Court determining civil liability under Section 154(5) and any excess deposit refunded. Merely because the Special Court is empowered to determine civil liability under Section 154(5) does not mean the authorities lack power to make a Section 126 assessment.

EA2003::174.code: Electricity Act, 2003 (with s.50; Supply Code Para 7.10 / 7.7.1-7.7.5)
EA2003::174.topic: Overriding effect of the Act does not oust Lok Adalat / Consumer Protection remedies for damages

cases.title: Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Others v. M/s Prakancha Metal Works Pvt. Ltd.
cases.topic: Overriding effect of the Act does not oust Lok Adalat / Consumer Protection remedies for damages
cases.holding: Section 174 gives the Act overriding effect only for matters provided under it; Section 50 does not empower the Supply Code to ascertain damages for a licensee's wrongful acts, and the Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum (Para 7.10, Clauses 7.7.1-7.7.5) covers only supply-related matters, not tortious damages for illegal disconnection. The Consumer Protection Act, 1986 is preserved (ss.173/174), and the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 (Lok Adalat) is a special Act for such damages; the Lok Adalat therefore had jurisdiction, to which the petitioners had in any event submitted.

EA2003::42.code: Electricity Act, 2003 (with UPERC CGRF & Ombudsman Regulations, 2007)
EA2003::42.topic: CGRF/Ombudsman cannot relegate a consumer's dispute to arbitration

cases.title: Executive Engineer, Electricity Urban Distribution Division v. The Electricity Ombudsman & 2 Others
cases.topic: CGRF/Ombudsman cannot relegate a consumer's dispute to arbitration
cases.holding: No. Under Section 42(5)-(8) and the Regulations, 2007, the ECGRF and Ombudsman are under a statutory duty to decide a consumer's grievance on merits; an arbitration clause in the agreement is at most an additional forum (Section 42(8) — without prejudice to other rights; right of election) and does not oust the statutory forum. The special statute overrides the general Arbitration Act. Regulation 5.1 bars the Forum only from matters under ss.126, 127, 128, 135-139, 143, 152 and 161; other disputes (Reg. 5.2) it must decide. The ECGRF erred in diverting the dispute to arbitration.
cases.flag: Maintainability: a writ by the Executive Engineer alone (an officer, not a juristic person) without the Distribution Licensee (PVVNL) was held not maintainable, but the Court decided on merits anyway (paras 62-63).

cases.title: Kisan Cold Storage & Ice Factory v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors. (Full Bench reference)
cases.topic: Only a consumer, not the Distribution Licensee, may approach the Electricity Ombudsman; Regulation 8.1(i) is ultra vires to the extent it includes the licensee
cases.holding: No. Section 42(5) constitutes the Forum for redressal of consumer grievances; Section 42(6) gives only a 'consumer' aggrieved by non-redressal the right to represent to the Ombudsman; Section 42(7) requires the Ombudsman to settle 'the grievance of the consumer'. The Act and Rule 7 of the Electricity Rules, 2005 nowhere contemplate a grievance-redressal remedy for the Distribution Licensee. Regulation 8.1(i) of the 2007 Regulations, in extending the Ombudsman remedy to the Distribution Licensee as well, is inconsistent with and therefore ultra vires Section 42(5)-(7) and Section 181(1) (regulations must be consistent with the Act); a statutory right of appeal/representation must be found in the statute itself, not manufactured by subordinate regulation.

cases.title: M.D., Pakshimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Electricity Ombudsman & Anr.
cases.topic: A licensee has no remedy of representation before the Ombudsman against a CGRF order
cases.holding: The licensee has no remedy to file a representation under Clause 8 of the 2007 Regulations read with Section 42(6) of the Act before the Ombudsman against an order of the CGRF, following Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Vidyut Lokpal, Lucknow (which struck down Clause 8 to that extent).

EA2003::43.clause: s.43 (duty to supply); reconnection vs fresh connection
EA2003::43.topic: Duty to supply is not absolute; consumer-premises synergy; reconnection = same premises

cases.title: K.C. Ninan v. Kerala State Electricity Board & Ors.
cases.neutral_citation: (2023) SCC OnLine SC 603; Civil Appeal Nos. 2109-2110 of 2004 (batch)
cases.topic: Duty to supply is not absolute; consumer-premises synergy; reconnection = same premises
cases.holding: The duty to supply under s.43 is not absolute and is subject to the charges and compliances stipulated by the utility as part of the application for supply; it is owed to the owner or occupier of particular premises, and one becomes a 'consumer' only with respect to those premises for which electricity is sought and provided. An application for the same premises for which supply was earlier provided is a 'reconnection'; different premises make it a fresh connection even if the consumer is the same.

EA2003::46.code: Electricity Act, 2003 (read with Clauses 4.6 & 4.21, Supply Code 2005)
EA2003::46.topic: Recoverable expenditure — actual expenses proved vs the licensee's own statutory obligation

cases.title: Suman Engineering and Chemicals Pvt. Ltd. v. U.P.P.C.L. & 4 Others
cases.topic: Recoverable expenditure — actual expenses proved vs the licensee's own statutory obligation
cases.holding: Under Section 46 a licensee may recover only “expenses reasonably incurred in providing any electric line or electrical plant”, and the burden to prove actual expenditure lies on the licensee (as the Supreme Court's remand directed). Extension of distribution mains and commissioning of new sub-stations is the licensee's own statutory obligation under the first proviso to Section 43(1) and cannot be loaded onto the consumer. On the evidence the 4-pole structure and service line were actually constructed, so Rs. 5,49,181 and Rs. 4,65,000 were rightly retained; the processing fee of Rs. 5,000 is non-refundable per the Cost Data Book.
cases.flag: The Supreme Court's remand order dated 29.11.2022 (in this very case) fixed the frame: refund is to be denied only “to the extent” the respondents prove “the actual expenses incurred.”

EA2003::56.topic: Recovery by suit is independent of the disconnection power

cases.title: K.C. Ninan v. Kerala State Electricity Board & Ors.
cases.neutral_citation: (2023) SCC OnLine SC 603; Civil Appeal Nos. 2109-2110 of 2004 (batch)
cases.topic: Recovery by suit is independent of the disconnection power
cases.holding: The power to initiate recovery proceedings by filing a suit against a defaulting consumer is independent of the power to disconnect supply as a means of recovery under Section 56.

EA2003::56(2).topic: Limitation on recovery — recurring companion provision in Supply Code litigation

cases.title: Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. v. State of U.P. & 3 Others
cases.topic: Limitation on recovery — recurring companion provision in Supply Code litigation
cases.holding: "Sum due" means an amount adjudicated between the parties; un-adjudicated, escalating demands raised years after the service ended are barred.
cases.flag: Respondent pleaded this as "Clause 56(2) of the U.P. Supply Code"; the provision quoted and applied is s.56(2) of the Act. Recorded, not merged.

cases.title: Assistant Engineer (D1), Ajmer Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Anr. v. Rahamatullah Khan alias Rahamjulla
cases.topic: Meaning of 'first due'; disconnection barred after two years but recovery not
cases.holding: 'First due' means when the bill is first issued (the liability arises on consumption but the sum becomes due only on billing). Section 56(2) bars only the remedy of disconnection after two years from the sum first becoming due (unless continuously shown as arrears); it does not bar a supplementary/additional demand or other modes of recovery. In a case of bona fide mistake, limitation for the additional demand runs from discovery (s.17(1)(c), Limitation Act, 1963), but the licensee still cannot disconnect supply — only pursue other recovery.

EA2003::64.topic: Truing up cannot change the methodology of the original tariff determination

cases.title: BSES Rajdhani Power Ltd. v. Delhi Electricity Regulatory Commission
cases.topic: Truing up cannot change the methodology of the original tariff determination
cases.holding: No. A tariff order under s.64 is quasi-judicial and binding until amended/revoked under s.64(6); truing up is only the adjustment of actuals against projections and cannot be used to re-think de novo the basic principles or retrospectively change the methodology of the initial determination. The DERC's changes on Issues 1, 2, 3 and 5 (LPSC/collection efficiency, depreciation, FR/SR salary, fringe benefit tax) were impermissible and are set aside; interest on Consumer Security Deposit (Issue 4) is a legitimate expense the appellants may recover.

JH-2005::9.2.code: Jharkhand SERC (Electricity Supply Code) Regulations, 2005 (framed under s.50, EA 2003)
JH-2005::9.2.topic: Reduction of contract demand — the 'initial period' runs from the initial agreement

cases.title: Jharkhand State Electricity Board & Others v. M/s Ramkrishna Forging Limited
cases.topic: Reduction of contract demand — the 'initial period' runs from the initial agreement
cases.holding: The initial agreement. Enhancement 'fresh agreements' for the same connection are merely supplementary amendments of the initial agreement (contract demand can be varied even by written communication, Reg. 2(l); reduction itself is by supplementary agreement, Reg. 9.2.6). So the three-year 'initial period' runs from the initial agreement (2004), not the last enhancement (2007); the 2007 reduction application was beyond it and is deemed allowed under Reg. 9.2. The Regulations are liberally construed for the consumer.

OFFTOPIC::criminal-interim.topic: Interlocutory stay in a s.482 complaint-quashing petition

cases.title: Dr. Vinod Kumar Bassi v. The State of U.P. & Anr.
cases.topic: Interlocutory stay in a s.482 complaint-quashing petition
cases.holding: On the applicant's contention that the complaint was proceeded with without the Section 202(1) Cr.P.C. enquiry (applicant residing in Lucknow, complaint filed in Hardoi), notice was ordered and further proceedings stayed till the next date. No merits were decided.
cases.flag: Off-topic for the Supply Code: a two-line interlocutory criminal order under Section 482 Cr.P.C.; no Electricity Supply Code provision is involved. Retained only for queue completeness.

OFFTOPIC::ipc-405-406-entrustment.code: Indian Penal Code, 1860 / Cr.P.C., 1973 (unrelated to the Electricity Act/Supply Code)
OFFTOPIC::ipc-405-406-entrustment.topic: Criminal breach of trust — commercial sale is not 'entrustment'; mandatory Section 202(1) enquiry

cases.title: Kishore Biyani v. State of U.P. & Anr.
cases.topic: Criminal breach of trust — commercial sale is not 'entrustment'; mandatory Section 202(1) enquiry
cases.holding: A mere commercial sale transaction (unpaid supply of goods) does not amount to 'entrustment' of property under Section 405 IPC; absent entrustment and dishonest misappropriation, no offence under Section 406 is made out. Where the accused resides outside the trial court's jurisdiction, Section 202(1) Cr.P.C. mandates an enquiry before summoning, and its omission vitiates the summoning order.
cases.flag: Entirely off-topic to the Supply Code jurisprudence; recorded only to keep the source-corpus review complete. No provision-holdings or authorities from this case are added to the Supply Code index.

OFFTOPIC::jurisdiction-not-by-consent.clause: no jurisdiction by consent, acquiescence, or waiver
OFFTOPIC::jurisdiction-not-by-consent.topic: Jurisdiction of a tribunal of limited/statutory jurisdiction cannot be conferred by consent, acquiescence, or an unreasoned prior order

cases.title: M.D., Pakshimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Electricity Ombudsman & Anr.
cases.topic: Jurisdiction of a tribunal of limited/statutory jurisdiction cannot be conferred by consent, acquiescence, or an unreasoned prior order
cases.holding: A tribunal or forum of limited/statutory jurisdiction cannot derive jurisdiction beyond the statute; no acquiescence, consent, or waiver can confer it, and a defect of jurisdiction cannot be cured even by consent, rendering any resulting order a nullity.

OFFTOPIC::landlord-tenant-civil.clause: Article 227; interim injunction to restore supply
OFFTOPIC::landlord-tenant-civil.topic: Restoration of a tenant's electric supply by civil injunction

cases.title: Dipali Dey (Baxi) v. Mira Das
cases.topic: Restoration of a tenant's electric supply by civil injunction
cases.holding: Where a tenant in possession has had supply disconnected by the landlord, the civil court may by injunction direct restoration pending the tenancy suit; the High Court should not interfere with such concurrent orders under Article 227. The tenancy dispute abides the trial.
cases.flag: Off-topic for the Supply Code: a Supreme Court order on a landlord-tenant civil injunction to restore supply; no Electricity Supply Code provision is construed. Retained as a node in the landlord-tenant disconnection line (cf. SCJ-016, SCJ-020).

OFFTOPIC::precedent-jindal-poly-films.clause: overruling a Division Bench decision that did not engage the specific statutory provision

cases.title: Kisan Cold Storage & Ice Factory v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors. (Full Bench reference)
cases.topic: Jindal Poly Films Ltd. overruled
cases.holding: The Division Bench in Jindal Poly Films Ltd. v. U.P. Electricity Regulatory Commission (15.4.2011) upheld Regulation 8.1(i) as intra vires on a general assertion that the Act should be read as a whole rather than section by section, without specifically engaging Section 42(5)-(7); that reasoning does not lay down the correct principle of law and is overruled.

cases.title: Gaya Prasad v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.topic: Empty listing order
cases.holding: At the petitioner's request the case was passed over for the day and listed in the next cause list; nothing was decided.
cases.flag: No substantive content: a bare pass-over/listing order with no Supply Code (or any) determination. Retained only for queue completeness.

OFFTOPIC::service-law-natural-justice.code: Service law / departmental inquiry (not the Supply Code)
OFFTOPIC::service-law-natural-justice.topic: Burden on the Establishment to prove charges in a major-penalty inquiry

cases.title: Dhirendra Kumar Chaudhary v. State of U.P. & 5 Others
cases.topic: Burden on the Establishment to prove charges in a major-penalty inquiry
cases.holding: In a departmental inquiry carrying a major penalty, the Establishment must prove the charges by leading documentary and oral evidence through a Presenting Officer, with witnesses offered for cross-examination, before an inquiry tribunal that distances itself from the Establishment; relying on mere complaints and considering material (further inquiry/I.T.-cell reports) behind the employee's back vitiates the proceedings for breach of natural justice. Dismissal quashed; reinstatement, with liberty to hold a fresh inquiry from the charge-sheet stage.
cases.flag: Off-topic for the Supply Code: this is a service/disciplinary matter. The Supply Code, 2005 appears only as the backdrop of the misconduct charge (irregular bill revisions); no Code provision is construed. Retained in the corpus for completeness (and for its authorities).

TORT::compensation-assessment.code: Law of torts / Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 (guidance)
TORT::compensation-assessment.clause: restitutio in integram; MV Act multiplier method
TORT::compensation-assessment.topic: Assessment of damages for electrocution disability

cases.title: Executive Engineer, Electricity Distribution Division-II v. State of U.P. & 2 Others
cases.topic: Assessment of damages for electrocution disability
cases.holding: Damages for loss of limb/life flow from tort principles (restitutio in integram); the Permanent Lok Adalat rightly took guidance from the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 second schedule / multiplier method to compute compensation for a 100% disability, and ~Rs. 21 lakh was not excessive. A departmental circular capping compensation at Rs. 2 lakh binds the Corporation's officials but not the court.

UP-2005::2(oo).topic: 'Occupier' requires authorised occupation — tenant under an unstayed eviction decree

cases.title: Dr. Ashok Kumar Sharma & Another v. State of U.P. & 4 Others
cases.topic: 'Occupier' requires authorised occupation — tenant under an unstayed eviction decree
cases.holding: A tenant is ordinarily an 'occupier' (Clause 2(oo)) entitled to apply for a connection on an indemnity bond and cannot be denied supply merely for want of the landlord's NOC. But 'occupier' means a person authorised to occupy; a tenant faced with an unstayed eviction decree is not so authorised, and the court declined, in its discretion under Article 226, to direct a connection at that stage — with liberty to apply if the decree is set aside, recalled or stayed.

UP-2005::2.2(tt).code: U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 (with UPERC Tariff Orders)
UP-2005::2.2(tt).topic: Protective-load charge requires the consumer's option and sanction

cases.title: Executive Engineer, Electricity Urban Distribution Division v. The Electricity Ombudsman & 2 Others
cases.topic: Protective-load charge requires the consumer's option and sanction
cases.holding: No. A 'Protective Load' (Clause 2.2(tt): a load not subject to normal rostering) charge under the Tariff Orders is attracted only where the consumer has opted for the facility and it has been sanctioned by the licensee. The Aviation College never exercised such option; the demand — raised suo motu for eight years' arrears on an audit objection — was illegal (following Allahabad Inter Prises v. State of U.P.).

UP-2005::4.1.topic: Arrears-bar is premises-specific; connection to a tenant/occupier of a distinct premises

cases.title: Anand Kumar v. State of U.P. & 2 Others
cases.topic: Arrears-bar is premises-specific; connection to a tenant/occupier of a distinct premises
cases.holding: No. The arrears-bar in the third proviso to Clause 4.1 applies only to dues on the same 'premises' (Clause 2(ss)); the shop is a distinct premises and the tenant is an 'occupier' (Clause 2(oo)) entitled to apply. Clause 4.3(h) forbids refusal on the ground of dues on other portions; the licensee must instead pursue the defaulters under Clause 4.3(f)(v).

cases.title: Chandra Prakash Gupta v. State of U.P. & 3 Others
cases.topic: Auction-purchaser and arrears — the Code as the missing statutory provision
cases.holding: No. Ahmedabad Electricity Co. v. Gujarat Inns turned on the absence of a statutory provision; Clause 4.1 of the 2005 Code (promulgated after that 2004 decision) now supplies one, requiring a No-Dues Certificate before a fresh connection on premises where ownership has changed and arrears exist. A SARFAESI auction-purchaser is bound by it and may obtain a connection only on furnishing a No-Dues Certificate.

UP-2005::4.21(a).topic: System-loading charges — refundability where the connection is cancelled and never energised

cases.title: Suman Engineering and Chemicals Pvt. Ltd. v. U.P.P.C.L. & 4 Others
cases.topic: System-loading charges — refundability where the connection is cancelled and never energised
cases.holding: Yes, refundable. A system-loading charge is a compulsory exaction on one who enjoys the benefit of the distribution system; the liability accrues only once the applicant starts consuming electricity using the licensee's system. A prospective consumer who never takes supply cannot be fastened with it. Refund of Rs. 32,00,000 with interest @ 8.5% p.a. from the date of deposit ordered.

cases.title: Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. v. State of U.P. & 3 Others
cases.topic: Parallel-operating charges under pre-existing ("old") agreements
cases.holding: No. The clause preserves the charge only till termination and is read subject to the maxim that no party may take advantage of its own wrong. Charges end with actual disconnection (28.9.2007); the demand for January 2008-30.11.2018, with interest, is quashed.

UP-2005::4.3(f).topic: Liability of an auction-purchaser for arrears attaching to the premises

cases.title: Amir Ahmad v. State of U.P. & 4 Others
cases.topic: Liability of an auction-purchaser for arrears attaching to the premises
cases.holding: Yes. Clause 4.3(f)(i) & (viii) place the duty to ascertain and clear outstanding dues on both seller and purchaser and permit the application to be processed only on clearance. The auction-purchaser, buying 'as-is-where-is', is fixed with 'buyer beware' and cannot escape the statutory charge by relying on the encumbrance-free recital or the vendor's non-consumption.

cases.title: Jitendra Kumar Gupta & Anr. v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.topic: Subsequent purchaser liable for premises dues, including a theft assessment
cases.holding: Yes. 'Outstanding dues' under Clause 4.3(f) means all dues pending on the premises, including a post-theft assessment, and attach to the premises; the purchaser must obtain a No-Dues Certificate. The theft being a personal criminal liability of the previous occupant does not exclude the assessed civil amount. But recovery from the purchaser is subject to adjustment against any amount recovered from the original defaulter (no double recovery); here, a practical direction to deposit 50% to obtain the connection.

UP-2005::4.3(g).topic: Pro-rata apportionment of arrears on a sub-divided premises

cases.title: Anubhav Jaiswal v. State of U.P. & 4 Others
cases.topic: Pro-rata apportionment of arrears on a sub-divided premises
cases.holding: Only his pro-rata share. Though outstanding dues are the first charge on the premises (Clause 4.3(f)(iv)), on a legal sub-division they are apportioned pro-rata (Clause 4.3(g)) and a connection to the sub-divided portion is given on payment of that portion's share alone (Clause 4.3(h)); the licensee cannot demand the whole. The matter is remanded for fresh pro-rata determination after notice to the original owner.

UP-2005::4.37.topic: Minimum-guarantee charges on temporary disconnection — only for consumer's default

cases.title: Harihar Cold Storage v. P.V.V.N.L. & Another
cases.topic: Minimum-guarantee charges on temporary disconnection — only for consumer's default
cases.holding: No. Clause 4.37 permits minimum-charge billing on a temporary disconnection only where the disconnection is on account of the consumer's default; here the disconnection was due to a burnt transformer the licensee failed to repair for about five months (breaching Clause 7.07's 24-hour restoration / 15-day replacement norms), so no minimum-guarantee charges lie. Where no fixed minimum sum is committed, minimum-guarantee charges require the licensee to ensure the minimum guaranteed supply.

UP-2005::4.4.topic: Tenant's connection on an indemnity bond absent owner's consent

cases.title: Anand Kumar v. State of U.P. & 2 Others
cases.topic: Tenant's connection on an indemnity bond absent owner's consent
cases.holding: Following Seema Mansoor, an occupier (including a tenant) has a statutory right to supply under Sections 42-43 read with Clause 4.4; where the owner's consent is unavailable, the tenant may file an indemnity bond (Annexure 4.2) to obtain the connection.

cases.title: Devendra Sharma v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.topic: Clause 4.4 governs new connections, not disconnection over a landlord-tenant dispute
cases.holding: No. Clause 4.4 applies to new-connection applications, not to disconnecting an existing connection. A landlord-tenant dispute is not a ground to cut a valid connection on which bills are paid; a connection may be disconnected only on grounds authorised by the Act/Code (theft, unauthorised use, non-payment). The disconnection here was illegal, arbitrary and malafide, and offended Article 21.

cases.title: Divya Sahani v. State of U.P. & Another
cases.topic: Pendency of a property dispute is not a ground to refuse/disconnect a connection
cases.holding: No. Clause 4.4 does not prohibit a connection because of a pending property dispute; Clause 4.4(a)(i) only requires that a court-order copy be furnished where ownership is in litigation. A connection is not proof of title (Note-3, Annexure 4.1). Disconnection solely for the pendency of a suit is dehors the law and violates Article 21; mandamus issued to grant the connection.

cases.title: Gaurav Sharma v. State of U.P. & 4 Others
cases.topic: Connection to a genuine occupier on an indemnity bond, without the owner's NOC
cases.holding: No. Section 43(1) confers on an occupier a statutory right to supply; Clause 4.4 read with Annexure 4.2 lets a genuine occupier unable to obtain the owner's NOC furnish an indemnity bond and obtain a connection. The object of the bond is only to exclude a trespasser/house-grabber; a family dispute or want of the owner's consent is no ground to refuse. Refusal quashed and remitted for reconsideration.

cases.title: Husna Bano v. State of U.P. & 9 Others
cases.topic: Tenant/occupier's connection on an indemnity bond amid a landlord-tenant dispute
cases.holding: No. Annexure 4.2 (Clause 4.4) enables an occupier who cannot obtain the owner's NOC to obtain a connection on an indemnity bond; possession can be shown by a Ration Card and Aadhaar (cash rent often leaving no receipt). The bond is not a document of title, and a connection does not bar an eviction suit; the landlord's refusal of NOC is no ground to deny supply. Refusal set aside and remitted for reconsideration.

UP-2005::4.49.topic: Load reduction with disputed arrears — Bond acceptable; effective date; agreed reduction cannot be defeated

cases.title: Kanpur Electricity Supply Co. Ltd. & Anr. v. M/s L.M.L. Limited & Ors.
cases.topic: Load reduction with disputed arrears — Bond acceptable; effective date; agreed reduction cannot be defeated
cases.holding: No. The unamended Clause 4.49 (in force on 19.4.2006) allowed the consumer to secure disputed arrears by a Bank Guarantee OR a Bond OR any instrument to the licensee's satisfaction; the reduction took effect from the first day of the month after sanction (Clause 4.41(e), i.e. 1.5.2006). Having agreed to the reduction and known of the consumer's Relief-Undertaking/Sick-Company status and the BIFR order, the licensee acted unfairly in rejecting the Bond, insisting on a Bank Guarantee and continuing to bill on the higher (8 MVA) load; the load stood reduced.

UP-2005::5.6(d).topic: Meter-testing procedure vs a compounded theft offence

cases.title: Abhinav Seva Sansthan Mahavidyalaya v. U.P. Power Corporation Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.topic: Meter-testing procedure vs a compounded theft offence
cases.holding: No. Once the sum is paid under Section 152(1) and the offence is deemed compounded, the tampering stands admitted-compounded and the question of following the meter-testing procedure (para 5.6(d)) does not arise. The theft assessment was made on the Code's formula (Annexure 6.3); the procedural challenge fails.

UP-2005::6.1(g).topic: Billing/disconnection window — 15-day bill dispatch plus disconnection notice

cases.title: Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Others v. M/s Prakancha Metal Works Pvt. Ltd.
cases.topic: Billing/disconnection window — 15-day bill dispatch plus disconnection notice
cases.holding: No. Clause 6.1(g) requires the bill to be dispatched at least 15 days before the due date, and a further seven days' notice is contemplated before disconnection; here the bill (issued 28.03.2011, due 31.03.2011) gave only three days and the disconnection (08.04.2011) preceded the statutory window, rendering it illegal. Ante-dating the payment receipt to 31.03.2011 was also illegal manipulation of the record.

UP-2005::6.14.topic: Consumer may seek payment of outstanding dues in installments under Clause 6.14

cases.title: Kripa Shanker v. State of U.P. Thru. Distt. Collector, Unnao & Ors.
cases.topic: Consumer may seek payment of outstanding dues in installments under Clause 6.14
cases.holding: Clause 6.14 of the Code already provides for payment of outstanding dues in installments; on an application by the consumer, the Executive Engineer must consider and decide the request expeditiously. By consent, the Court directed the petitioner to deposit Rs. 15,000 and move a Clause 6.14 application, staying recovery pending decision, conditional on the deposit being made.

UP-2005::6.16.topic: Protective treatment of sick industrial companies / relief undertakings

cases.title: Kanpur Electricity Supply Co. Ltd. & Anr. v. M/s L.M.L. Limited & Ors.
cases.topic: Protective treatment of sick industrial companies / relief undertakings
cases.holding: Clauses 4.41 and 4.49 are Rules framed to help industries in difficulty; read with Annexure 6.5 / Clause 6.16 (disconnected units seeking revival) and Clause 9.5 (Relief Undertaking regime under s.23), only current dues are realized from a sick/relief undertaking, with past dues recovered in instalments and no coercive disconnection — harmonised with the BIFR/SICA order.

UP-2005::6.5.topic: Billing disputes — alternative remedy of complaint before the Competent Authority

cases.title: Chandrika v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.topic: Billing disputes — alternative remedy of complaint before the Competent Authority
cases.holding: A dispute as to the correctness of a bill is to be raised by complaint before the Competent Authority (the Executive Engineer) under Clause 6.5 of the Code; the writ petition is disposed of by relegating the consumer to that remedy, with a direction to decide by a speaking order after hearing and interim protection from coercive recovery conditioned on a part-deposit (Rs. 20,000).

cases.title: Lala Ram Batham v. U.P. Power Corporation Nigam & Ors.
cases.topic: Disputed meter reading relegated to a Clause 6.5 representation, with mandatory inspection of the removed meter
cases.holding: Under Clause 6.5 of the Code, the consumer may raise the grievance by representation before the licensee, who must decide it expeditiously by a speaking order after hearing the consumer; before deciding, the licensee must personally inspect the removed (old) meter to verify the correctness of the disputed reading. The writ court did not adjudicate the claim on merits.

UP-2005::6.8.topic: Reasonable opportunity of hearing before a theft-based final assessment; procedural defect condoned where opportunity was in substance given

cases.title: Lalit Kumar Kapoor v. Kanpur Electricity Supply Company & Anr.
cases.topic: Reasonable opportunity of hearing before a theft-based final assessment; procedural defect condoned where opportunity was in substance given
cases.holding: Reasonable opportunity of hearing in a theft assessment is governed by Clauses 6.8(b)(i), 6.8(c)(iii) read with 8.1(b) of the Code (citing Khem Chand v. Union of India and Transmission Corporation of A.P. v. Sri Rama Krishna Rice Mill on the nature of 'reasonable opportunity'). Provisional assessment, reply, and final assessment together form a single process reaching finality; where the authority afforded an opportunity for hearing (including through consideration of a representation directed by an earlier writ order) before making the final assessment, any procedural defect at the provisional stage is condoned, since procedural law cannot override the substantive law.

cases.title: Latif v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.topic: Mandatory Clause 6.8 procedure for unauthorised-use assessment; bypassing it via the 1958 Recovery of Dues Act is illegal
cases.holding: No. Following Ashok Kumar & Others v. State of U.P., Clause 6.8 requires: (a) a site inspection report disclosing the irregularity, handed to the consumer or pasted/posted if refused; (b) a show-cause notice with the provisional assessment, giving 15 working days for reply and fixing a hearing date; and (c) after personal hearing, a speaking final order within 7 working days recording whether unauthorised use is established and the assessed amount. Since no such show-cause notice was issued and no final order under Clause 6.8(c) was passed, a bill-cum-notice and demand notice issued instead under Section 5 of the 1958 Act is illegal and inconsistent with the prescribed procedure; it is set aside, without prejudice to the licensee proceeding afresh in accordance with the Clause 6.8/Ashok Kumar procedure.

UP-2005::6.8(d).code: U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 (read with s.127, Electricity Act 2003)
UP-2005::6.8(d).topic: Remedy against a final theft assessment — statutory appeal under s.127 / Clause 6.8(d)

cases.title: Dr. Santosh Kumar Awasthi v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.topic: Remedy against a final theft assessment — statutory appeal under s.127 / Clause 6.8(d)
cases.holding: The remedy against a final order of assessment is the statutory appeal under Section 127 read with Clause 6.8(d) of the Code, on deposit of half the assessed amount; the writ court relegated the consumer to that appeal, directing it be entertained without a limitation objection, staying recovery for 30 days, and leaving the merits and any stay to the appellate authority.

UP-2005::6.9.code: U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 (with s.126, EA 2003 & Tariff Order)
UP-2005::6.9.topic: Excess load / appliance installation is not 'unauthorised use' under Section 126

cases.title: Kanpur Electricity Supply Co. Ltd. & Anr. v. U.P. Electricity Regulatory Commission & Ors.
cases.topic: Excess load / appliance installation is not 'unauthorised use' under Section 126
cases.holding: It is not Section 126 unauthorised use. Para 6.9 of the Code provides that excess load is not covered by Section 126; the use of an air conditioner is not prohibited but attracts an additional Fixed Charge under the tariff (Rs. 150 per ton, April-September). The CGRF/Ombudsman rightly disallowed the Section 126 assessment and permitted only supplementary Fixed-Charge bills.

UP-2005::7.10.code: U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 (with s.42(5)-(7), EA 2003; UPERC (CGRF & Ombudsman) Regulations)
UP-2005::7.10.topic: Only the consumer, not the Distribution Licensee, may approach the Forum or the Ombudsman

cases.title: M.K. Pathak, Executive Engineer v. The Electricity Ombudsman & Ors.
cases.topic: Only the consumer, not the Distribution Licensee, may approach the Forum or the Ombudsman
cases.holding: No. Clause 7.10 of the Code and Section 42(5)-(7) of the Act, on a plain reading, entitle only the consumer to file a complaint before the Forum and, if aggrieved by non-redressal, a representation before the Ombudsman; this right is not given to the Electricity Distribution Licensee. The licensee/its officers therefore have no authority in law to approach the Ombudsman once the Forum has decided the consumer's complaint, and the Ombudsman commits no error of law in dismissing such a representation, even on its merits.

UP-2005::8.1.code: U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 (with s.126, EA 2003 & 1958 Dues Recovery Act)
UP-2005::8.1.topic: Proper assessment (with hearing) is a precondition to recovery

cases.title: Gauri Shankar Gupta v. State of U.P. & 4 Others
cases.topic: Proper assessment (with hearing) is a precondition to recovery
cases.holding: No. Clause 8.1(a)&(b) read with Section 126 require notice, service of the provisional assessment, and an opportunity of hearing before a final assessment; only on such an assessment, and non-payment of the demand thereunder, can recourse be had to the 1958 Act. The department failed to show the demand notice was served or that any assessment order was passed; the recovery order and citation are quashed, with liberty to reassess after hearing.

UP-2005::8.1(b)(iii).topic: Theft assessment — mandatory 15-day provisional-bill notice before final assessment

cases.title: Chunni Lal Gupta v. State of U.P. & 2 Others
cases.topic: Theft assessment — mandatory 15-day provisional-bill notice before final assessment
cases.holding: No. Clause 8.1(b)(iii) requires service of a provisional assessment bill with 15 days to reply and a hearing before final assessment. A 'revised bill' issued on the day of the raid, without that procedure, cannot be a final assessment; it is at best provisional, the consumer may file objections to be decided per the Code, and may appeal under Section 127 thereafter.

cases.title: Dr. Munni Lal v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.topic: Theft assessment — mandatory 15-working-day show-cause notice and hearing
cases.holding: No. Clause 8.1(b)(iii) requires a show-cause notice giving 15 working days to object and fixing a hearing date before a final assessment; a seven-day notice with no hearing date does not comply. No final order of assessment was passed, so the recovery demand was premature.

UP-2005::compounding.topic: Theft (s.135) compounded through the Supply Code — theft/UUE-Code linkage

cases.title: Ajmal v. State of U.P. & 2 Ors.
cases.topic: Theft (s.135) compounded through the Supply Code — theft/UUE-Code linkage
cases.holding: The offence of electricity theft under Section 135 being compoundable, the accused's compounding remedy lies 'as provided under the provisions of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005' — the Code furnishing the machinery through which theft (Section 135) and, cognately, unauthorised use of electricity (Section 126) are assessed and compounded. Pending compounding, as the offence does not entail imprisonment beyond seven years, any arrest must comply with Section 41(1)(b) read with Section 41-A Cr.P.C.; the FIR, disclosing a cognizable offence, was not quashed.
cases.flag: Scope: the case's express Code engagement is the compounding remedy; the operative relief concerned arrest safeguards (s.41(1)(b)/41-A Cr.P.C.). Retained as a node in the theft / unauthorised-use line, which the Supply Code's assessment and compounding machinery governs.

UP-2005::tariff-feeder.clause: feeder-based tariff; set-off of repair cost
UP-2005::tariff-feeder.topic: Rural-feeder supply cannot be billed at urban rate; no self-help set-off

cases.title: Harihar Cold Storage v. P.V.V.N.L. & Another
cases.topic: Rural-feeder supply cannot be billed at urban rate; no self-help set-off
cases.holding: Supply made from a rural feeder cannot be billed at the urban-feeder rate schedule (conceded); the excess is refundable. A consumer who, without authorisation, gets the transformer repaired at his own cost cannot set off that cost against his bills — the remedy is a civil suit.

UPDR1958::3.code: U.P. Government Electrical Undertaking (Dues Recovery) Act, 1958
UPDR1958::3.topic: Recovery demand presupposes a final assessment

cases.title: Dr. Munni Lal v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.topic: Recovery demand presupposes a final assessment
cases.holding: A demand under Section 3 of the 1958 Dues Recovery Act can be issued only after a final order of assessment is passed; a demand issued before final assessment is without authority and is quashed.

WB-2004::5.2.code: West Bengal Electricity Regulatory Commission (Electricity Supply Code) Regulations, 2004
WB-2004::5.2.topic: Disconnection procedure and the statutory route of objection/appeal under ss.126-127

cases.title: Chairman, West Bengal State Electricity Board & Ors. v. Syed Mukbul Hossain & Ors.
cases.topic: Disconnection procedure and the statutory route of objection/appeal under ss.126-127
cases.holding: Disconnection of supply on a theft allegation must follow the procedure of Regulation 5.2; the consumer's remedies are to object under Section 126(3) before the final assessment and to appeal the final order under Section 127. As the final assessment had already been made, the Court relegated the parties to the statutory appeal, to be decided on merits (including the maintainability/limitation objection), setting aside the costs and interim directions of the High Court and expressing no opinion on merits.
cases.flag: Multi-state: construes the West Bengal Supply Code (2004), not the U.P. 2005 Code. The Supreme Court expressly decided nothing on the merits.

cases.title: Executive Engineer, Southern Electricity Supply Co. of Orissa Ltd. (SOUTHCO) v. Sri Seetaram Rice Mill
cases.application: Foundational: Section 126 (civil, no mens rea, wider purposive 'unauthorised use' covering excess load/change of category under Explanation (b)(iv)) and Section 135 (criminal, mens rea) operate in different and distinct fields with no commonality; Sections 126-127 are a complete code, only the final Section 126(3) order is appealable, and Article 226 relief is confined to jurisdictional review.

cases.title: West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd. (WBSEDCL) v. M/s Orion Metal Pvt. Ltd.
cases.application: Theft (s.135) is a subset of unauthorised use (s.126); a s.126 assessment is available even in theft cases, requiring only civil proof (not proof beyond reasonable doubt/mens rea), and does not merge into or get ousted by the Special Court's s.154(5) civil-liability jurisdiction — both may run in parallel. Applies and extends Seetaram Rice Mill.

lead_authorities.name: Executive Engineer (SOUTHCO) v. Sri Seetaram Rice Mill

cases.title: Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. v. State of U.P. & 3 Others
cases.application: Bars the consumer's refund of charges paid without demur and the licensee that only raised bills, never pursuing statutory recovery (s.52 noted).

cases.title: Kapil Gupta v. U.P. Power Corpn. Ltd. & Anr.
cases.application: A writ against a Section 126 assessment is relegated to the Section 127 appeal unless the case falls within the jurisdiction / natural-justice / fundamental-rights exceptions; pure factual disputes go to the appeal.

lead_authorities.name: Ashok Kumar v. State of U.P.
M/s Popcorn Entertainment v. City Industrial Development Corporation

cases.title: Anubhav Jaiswal v. State of U.P. & 4 Others
cases.application: On a legal sub-division of a premises, outstanding electricity dues are divided pro-rata; a purchaser of a portion is liable only for that portion's share.

cases.title: Anand Kumar v. State of U.P. & 2 Others
cases.application: The bar on a new connection for arrears attaches only to the specific premises in default, not to other portions of a building.

cases.title: Amir Ahmad v. State of U.P. & 4 Others
cases.application: Electricity arrears create a statutory charge on the premises recoverable from a subsequent transferee, including an auction-purchaser on an 'as-is-where-is' basis.

lead_authorities.name: K.C. Ninan v. Kerala State Electricity Board

cases.title: Chandra Prakash Gupta v. State of U.P. & 3 Others
cases.application: The 2005 Code creates the statutory charge that the pre-Code case law lacked: an auction-purchaser cannot escape the previous owner's arrears and must furnish a No-Dues Certificate for a fresh connection.

lead_authorities.name: Ahmedabad Electricity Co. Ltd. v. Gujarat Inns Pvt. Ltd.

cases.title: Haryana State Electricity Board v. M/s Hanuman Rice Mills, Dhanauri & Ors.
cases.application: Electricity arrears are not a charge on the premises; a transferee/auction-purchaser is liable for the previous owner's dues only where statutory rules or statutory conditions of supply expressly so provide (the refinement underlying the K.C. Ninan line).

lead_authorities.name: Isha Marbles v. Bihar State Electricity Board
Dakshin Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Paramount Polymers (P) Ltd.
Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. DVS Steels & Alloys (P) Ltd.

cases.title: Jitendra Kumar Gupta & Anr. v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.application: 'Outstanding dues' on a premises (including a theft assessment) attach to the premises and are recoverable from a subsequent purchaser, who must obtain a No-Dues Certificate — subject to adjustment against recovery from the original defaulter.

cases.title: K.C. Ninan v. Kerala State Electricity Board & Ors.
cases.neutral_citation: (2023) SCC OnLine SC 603; Civil Appeal Nos. 2109-2110 of 2004 (batch)
cases.application: Apex authority: the Supply Code (under s.50/s.181) can create a statutory charge on the premises for a previous owner's arrears recoverable from a new/subsequent owner; a condition requiring a new owner to clear such arrears is statutory and valid (confirming and extending Haryana SEB v. Hanuman Rice Mills; substantially qualifying Isha Marbles).

lead_authorities.name: Isha Marbles v. Bihar State Electricity Board

cases.title: Islam v. State of U.P. & 4 Others
cases.application: In a theft/unauthorised-use assessment the burden is on the department to prove commercial or unauthorised use; a farmer need not disprove it where his use is ancillary agricultural use within the sanctioned load.

cases.title: M.D., Pakshimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Electricity Ombudsman & Anr.
cases.application: CGRF/Ombudsman (creatures of subordinate regulation) have no jurisdiction to review a statutory Assessing Officer's Section 126 assessment or a Section 127 appellate order; the only remedy against such an assessment is under Sections 126/127 themselves. Anchors the later Full Bench holding (SCJ-043 Kisan Cold Storage) that the Ombudsman/CGRF scheme is a distinct consumer-grievance track confined to matters outside Sections 126/127/135 etc.

lead_authorities.name: Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Vidyut Lokpal, Lucknow

cases.title: Aruna Bhargava v. PuVVNL & Another
cases.application: A change of forum is not a matter of pure procedure; once proceedings are validly initiated before a forum, that vested right continues despite a later change of jurisdiction, unless the legislature clearly provides otherwise.

lead_authorities.name: CIT v. R. Sharadamma
CIT v. Dhadi Sahu

cases.title: Suman Engineering and Chemicals Pvt. Ltd. v. U.P.P.C.L. & 4 Others
cases.application: Liability for system-upgradation (the system-loading charge) accrues only on actual consumption; a prospective consumer who never draws supply bears no share of it.

cases.title: Executive Engineer, Electricity Urban Distribution Division v. The Electricity Ombudsman & 2 Others
cases.application: A tariff charge conditioned on the consumer opting for a facility (here, protective load) cannot be levied absent that option and the licensee's sanction; it cannot be imposed suo motu on an audit objection.

cases.title: Latif v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.application: The Clause 6.8 inspection-notice-hearing-final-order sequence is mandatory before any unauthorised-use assessment; a demand raised by bypassing this procedure (e.g. directly under the 1958 Recovery of Dues Act) is illegal, following and applying Ashok Kumar v. State of U.P.

lead_authorities.name: Ashok Kumar & Others v. State of U.P. & Others

cases.title: Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Others v. M/s Prakancha Metal Works Pvt. Ltd.
cases.application: The Code's grievance forum (CGRF/Ombudsman) and the Act's overriding clause do not cover a claim of tortious damages for wrongful disconnection; such claims lie before the Lok Adalat / consumer fora.

cases.title: Divisional Engineer, Electricity Distribution Division-I v. Raman Singh & Another
cases.application: The Supply Code and its CGRF/Ombudsman forum cover consumer grievances, not a non-consumer's tort-damages claim against the licensee; such claims lie before the Permanent Lok Adalat as a public-utility-service dispute.

lead_authorities.name: Bar Council of India v. Union of India
S.N. Pandey v. Union of India

cases.title: Executive Engineer, Electricity Distribution Division-II v. State of U.P. & 2 Others
cases.application: The Supply Code/EA scheme (and the s.145 civil-court bar) govern consumer disputes; a non-consumer's tort-damages claim for electrocution is a public-utility-service dispute the Permanent Lok Adalat may decide.

lead_authorities.name: Bar Council of India v. Union of India
United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Ajay Sinha

cases.title: Jharkhand State Electricity Board & Others v. M/s Ramkrishna Forging Limited
cases.application: Supply Code regulations, being terms dictated by a monopoly supplier, are to be liberally interpreted in favour of the consumer; load-enhancement agreements are treated as continuations of the initial agreement.

cases.title: Assistant Engineer (D1), Ajmer Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Anr. v. Rahamatullah Khan alias Rahamjulla
cases.application: The two-year bar in s.56(2) restricts only the coercive remedy of disconnection; the licensee may still raise a supplementary demand and pursue other modes of recovery (including within limitation from discovery of a mistake).

cases.title: Devendra Sharma v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.application: A landlord-tenant or ownership dispute is not a ground to disconnect a validly sanctioned electricity connection; the Code's new-connection procedure cannot be turned to that use.

cases.title: Dipali Dey (Baxi) v. Mira Das
cases.application: A tenant in possession is not to be deprived of electric supply on account of a landlord-tenant dispute; supply is restored (here by civil injunction pending the suit).

cases.title: Divya Sahani v. State of U.P. & Another
cases.application: A pending ownership/property dispute is not a ground to refuse or disconnect a connection; a connection confers no title, so the supply question is independent of the title dispute.

cases.title: Kanpur Electricity Supply Co. Ltd. & Anr. v. U.P. Electricity Regulatory Commission & Ors.
cases.application: Excess load or appliance installation within/around the contracted load is not 'unauthorised use' under Section 126 (para 6.9 of the Code); the remedy is the tariff's additional Fixed Charge, not a theft/UUE assessment.

cases.title: Assistant Engineer (D1), Ajmer Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Anr. v. Rahamatullah Khan alias Rahamjulla
cases.application: Electricity charges become 'first due' when the bill is issued quantifying them, though liability to pay arises on consumption; the limitation clock under s.56(2) starts from billing.

cases.title: Divisional Engineer, Electricity Distribution Division-I v. Raman Singh & Another
cases.application: Electricity distribution is a hazardous activity; the licensee is under a statutory duty to maintain its installations and lines so that passers-by (human or animal) are not harmed.

lead_authorities.name: Shakuntala Devi v. Delhi Electric Supply Undertaking

cases.title: Executive Engineer, Electricity Distribution Division-II v. State of U.P. & 2 Others
cases.application: A distribution company has an onerous duty to maintain its devices and to disconnect current from the sub-station in a storm; failure to do so is negligence founding a damages claim.

cases.title: Kripa Shanker v. State of U.P. Thru. Distt. Collector, Unnao & Ors.
cases.application: A consumer unable to pay an outstanding bill in one go may apply under Clause 6.14 of the Supply Code for installment payment; the Executive Engineer must consider and decide such an application expeditiously.

cases.title: Lalit Kumar Kapoor v. Kanpur Electricity Supply Company & Anr.
cases.application: For determining which version of Section 126 (deposit condition, assessment rate) applies, the operative date is the date of the FINAL assessment, not the provisional assessment or the date the cause of action arose.

lead_authorities.name: Sri Bhagwan Gupta v. Kanpur Electricity Supply Company Ltd.

cases.title: BSES Rajdhani Power Ltd. v. Delhi Electricity Regulatory Commission
cases.application: When the Supply Code / Section 126 deems assessed energy to be consumed, the fiction must be given full effect and the assessed units treated as sales.

cases.title: Suman Engineering and Chemicals Pvt. Ltd. v. U.P.P.C.L. & 4 Others
cases.application: Deposits taken as part of the estimate are refundable unless the licensee proves the actual expenditure reasonably incurred; unproved heads must be refunded.

cases.title: Lala Ram Batham v. U.P. Power Corporation Nigam & Ors.
cases.application: A disputed/implausible meter reading is to be resolved by a Clause 6.5 representation before the licensee, decided by a speaking order after inspection of the meter, rather than by the writ court on merits.

cases.title: Dhirendra Kumar Chaudhary v. State of U.P. & 5 Others
cases.application: The Establishment must prove disciplinary charges by evidence led through a Presenting Officer; charges are not proof of themselves, and material used behind the delinquent's back vitiates the inquiry.

lead_authorities.name: State of U.P. v. Saroj Kumar Sinha
Roop Singh Negi v. Punjab National Bank
State of Uttaranchal v. Kharak Singh

cases.title: Harihar Cold Storage v. P.V.V.N.L. & Another
cases.application: Minimum-guarantee (and like) charges cannot be levied for a period in which supply failed for a reason attributable to the licensee; the obligation to pay is tied to the licensee's maintaining the minimum standard of supply.

lead_authorities.name: Raymond Ltd. v. M.P. Electricity Board

cases.title: Gaurav Sharma v. State of U.P. & 4 Others
cases.application: A genuine occupier (including a family member in separate possession) has a statutory right under s.43(1) to a connection and may furnish an indemnity bond (Annexure 4.2) where the owner's NOC is unavailable; the bond only excludes trespassers/house-grabbers.

lead_authorities.name: Seema Mansoor v. U.P. Power Corporation
Chandu Khamaru v. Nayan Malik

cases.title: Husna Bano v. State of U.P. & 9 Others
cases.application: A tenant/occupier unable to obtain the owner's NOC may obtain a connection on an indemnity bond (Annexure 4.2); the bond is not a title document, and a landlord-tenant/succession dispute is no ground to deny the basic necessity of electricity.

lead_authorities.name: Gaurav Sharma v. State of U.P.
Chandu Khamaru v. Nayan Malik

cases.title: Dr. Ashok Kumar Sharma & Another v. State of U.P. & 4 Others
cases.application: The right of a tenant/occupier to a connection under the Code presupposes authorised occupation; it does not extend to a person against whom an unstayed eviction decree operates. (Qualifies the tenant-occupier entitlement recognised in Anand Kumar / SCJ-006.)

lead_authorities.name: Anand Kumar v. State of U.P.

cases.title: Kisan Cold Storage & Ice Factory v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors. (Full Bench reference)
cases.application: Foundational Full Bench ruling: the Section 42(5)-(7) Forum/Ombudsman grievance scheme is for the consumer alone; a Regulation cannot extend the Ombudsman remedy to the Distribution Licensee, as that would make the subordinate regulation inconsistent with the parent Act.

lead_authorities.name: Jindal Poly Films Limited v. U.P. Electricity Regulatory Commission

cases.title: M.K. Pathak, Executive Engineer v. The Electricity Ombudsman & Ors.
cases.application: Confirms, on Clause 7.10 of the Supply Code and Section 42(5)-(7), that only the consumer (not the licensee) may approach the CGRF/Ombudsman — an independent DB ruling reaching the same conclusion later confirmed by the Full Bench in Kisan Cold Storage (SCJ-043) construing the parallel UPERC Regulations, 2007 provision.

cases.title: Chunni Lal Gupta v. State of U.P. & 2 Others
cases.application: A final theft/assessment bill cannot be raised without the Code's mandatory provisional-bill notice, 15-day reply window and hearing; a same-day 'revised bill' is only provisional.

cases.title: Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Others v. M/s Prakancha Metal Works Pvt. Ltd.
cases.application: The Code's billing/disconnection timeline (15-day bill dispatch plus notice) is mandatory; a truncated bill and premature disconnection are illegal.

cases.title: Dr. Munni Lal v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.application: A final theft assessment requires the Code's mandatory 15-working-day show-cause notice and a hearing; recovery cannot precede a final assessment.

cases.title: Gauri Shankar Gupta v. State of U.P. & 4 Others
cases.application: A proper Section 126 / Clause 8.1 assessment made after notice and hearing is a precondition to any recovery of theft dues; recovery under the 1958 Act cannot precede a valid final assessment.

cases.title: Hazi Mohd. Yaseen v. P.V.V.N.L. & Another
cases.application: In the consumer/electricity-theft context, the statutory 'reasonable opportunity of hearing' (s.126(3)) includes a personal hearing before a final assessment; taking note of written objections alone is insufficient.

lead_authorities.name: Transmission Corpn. of A.P. Ltd. v. Sri Rama Krishna Rice Mill
Khem Chand v. Union of India

cases.title: Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. v. State of U.P. & 3 Others
cases.application: Applied against a distribution licensee: the procedural prerequisite (amending the agreement) is deemed waived within a reasonable time of the consumer's request.

lead_authorities.name: M.K. Shah Engineers & Contractors v. State of M.P.
Kusheshwar Prasad Singh v. State of Bihar
Mrutunjay Pani v. Narmada Bala Sasmal
Chairman, SBI v. M.J. James
Nirmala Anand v. Advent Corporation (Pvt.) Ltd.

cases.title: Lalit Kumar Kapoor v. Kanpur Electricity Supply Company & Anr.
cases.application: Reasonable opportunity of hearing before a theft-based Section 126 assessment is governed by Clauses 6.8(b)(i)/6.8(c)(iii)/8.1(b) of the Supply Code; substantial compliance (even via a court-directed representation) condones a procedural defect at the provisional stage.

lead_authorities.name: Khem Chand v. Union of India
Transmission Corporation of A.P. Ltd. v. Sri Rama Krishna Rice Mill

cases.title: BSES Rajdhani Power Ltd. v. Delhi Electricity Regulatory Commission
cases.application: A Regulator cannot, at the truing-up stage, change the methodology or principles of the initial tariff determination; doing so is an impermissible retrospective revision of a quasi-judicial tariff order.

lead_authorities.name: PTC India Ltd. v. CERC

cases.title: Chairman, West Bengal State Electricity Board & Ors. v. Syed Mukbul Hossain & Ors.
cases.application: Where the statutory appeal under Section 127 against a final assessment is available and has been invoked, the parties are relegated to it (with maintainability/limitation left to the appellate authority) rather than to writ/appellate interference on merits.

cases.title: Chandrika v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.application: A billing-correctness dispute is to be pursued through the Code's grievance channel (Clause 6.5) before the Competent Authority, not by writ, the writ court granting only interim protection on part-deposit.

cases.title: Dr. Santosh Kumar Awasthi v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.application: Against a final theft-assessment order, the consumer is relegated to the s.127 / Clause 6.8(d) appeal (with the half-deposit), the writ court giving only limitation protection and a short recovery stay.

cases.title: Devendra Sharma v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.application: Supply of electricity is necessary for a life with dignity; disconnection for reasons not authorised by the Act/Code, for malafide purposes, violates Article 21.

cases.title: Divya Sahani v. State of U.P. & Another
cases.application: Supply of electricity to an occupant is fundamental to living with dignity under Article 21; refusal/disconnection on extraneous grounds offends it.

cases.title: Kanpur Electricity Supply Co. Ltd. & Anr. v. M/s L.M.L. Limited & Ors.
cases.application: A licensee must give protective, fair treatment to a Relief Undertaking / Sick Industrial Company (current dues only, arrears in instalments, no coercive disconnection) and cannot defeat an agreed load reduction by legalese; the Supply Code is applied to aid revival.

lead_authorities.name: Modern Syntax (I) Ltd. v. Debts Recovery Tribunal, Jaipur

cases.title: Executive Engineer, Electricity Urban Distribution Division v. The Electricity Ombudsman & 2 Others
cases.application: A statutory consumer grievance forum (CGRF/Ombudsman) must decide the consumer's dispute on merits and cannot abdicate by relegating the parties to an arbitration clause; the statutory remedy is additional, by right of election, not ousted by the agreement.

lead_authorities.name: Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Ltd. v. Essar Power Ltd.

cases.title: Ajmal v. State of U.P. & 2 Ors.
cases.application: A compoundable Section 135 theft offence is to be compounded under the Electricity Supply Code, 2005 procedure; the Code supplies the enforcement / compounding machinery for theft (and, cognately, unauthorised use under Section 126).

cases.title: Aruna Bhargava v. PuVVNL & Another
cases.application: The right of appeal is a substantive right that vests when the original (here, assessment) proceedings are initiated, governed by the law then in force, and is not taken away by a later statute unless expressly or by necessary intendment; a new pre-deposit condition cannot be imposed on such a vested appeal.

lead_authorities.name: Garikapati Veeraya v. N. Subbiah Choudhry
Ramesh Singh v. Cinta Devi
Shiv Shakti Coop. Housing Society v. Swaraj Developers

cases.title: Abhinav Seva Sansthan Mahavidyalaya v. U.P. Power Corporation Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.application: A compounding/assessment amount paid without protest or contemporaneous objection cannot later be assailed as realised under coercion.
